hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? is there something hard in your life right now that you can’t change?
options: i’m sorry. this story might help you carry it.
good. keep this one for later.

steps.line: In the Roman Empire, almost two thousand years ago, a boy from what’s now Turkey grew up enslaved. His name, Epictetus, means “acquired.” Bought.
An old story says his master once began twisting his leg. Epictetus looked up and said, quietly: “You will break it.”
steps.label: an old story

steps.q: The master keeps twisting, and the leg breaks. How does Epictetus speak to him now?
steps.why: He just says, “Didn’t I tell you that you would break it?” No scream, no curse. Epictetus was lame all his life, and later taught: lameness gets in the way of the leg, not of the will (Handbook 9).

steps.line: The master kept twisting, and the leg broke. Epictetus said, calmly: “Didn’t I tell you that you would break it?”
steps.label: an old story

steps.q: Why does Epictetus simply warn his master, instead of begging or fighting?
o: Begging would only have made it worse
He spoke the truth, and left the choice to him
He had trained himself not to feel pain
steps.why: What the master did was up to the master. What Epictetus said was up to Epictetus. It still hurt.

steps.line: To be honest about it: this story comes from one Roman writer, Celsus. Another old source says illness made him lame. No one knows for sure.
What is known: Epictetus was lame, was freed, and became a famous teacher. He taught: “Lameness is an impediment to the leg, but not to the will.”

steps.q: Epictetus never wrote a book. So how do we know what he taught?
o: He dictated letters to his friends
A student wrote down his talks
His former master kept a record
steps.why: His student Arrian wrote down his talks as the Discourses and boiled them into a little Handbook. James Stockdale, a US pilot, leaned on it through seven years as a prisoner of war.

steps.line: Today: a bad knee, a hard diagnosis, a person who won’t change. Some things aren’t yours to fix. The voice you answer in still is.
steps.label: today

steps.q: Free at last, Epictetus taught in Rome. Then the emperor banished the philosophers. What did he do?
o: Started a new school in Greece
steps.why: When Domitian expelled the philosophers, around 93 AD, he moved to Nicopolis in Greece and opened a school. Students sailed there from all over the empire.

say: here’s what i love. this isn’t about pretending pain doesn’t hurt, or that cruelty is fine. if it happened, it was wrong.
the stoics put it in one line: some things are up to you, and some are not. a twisted leg wasn’t his to stop. the voice he answered in was. he spent the rest of his life teaching that.

steps.q: His handbook begins: “Of things some are in our power, and others are not.” In the story, which one was in his power?
o: What his master chose to do
steps.why: Only his answer. That small piece was enough to build a whole life of teaching on.

today.say: today, try the first exercise of his handbook. take one worry and sort it, on paper if you like, into two short lists: up to me, and not up to me. then put your effort only into the first list. if it’s too much today, write just one line.
options: gently. that’s all he did, one answer at a time.
then just one line. that’s yours too.

card.keepWhy: The voice you answer in stays yours.
sources: Origen, Against Celsus 7.53: Celsus cites Epictetus, who, when his master was twisting his leg, said smiling and unmoved, “You will break it,” and when it was broken, “Did I not tell you that you would break it?”
Epictetus, Enchiridion 9 (George Long, 1877): “Lameness is an impediment to the leg, but not to the will”; Enchiridion 1: “Of things some are in our power, and others are not.”
His owner Epaphroditus, a freedman of Nero (named in the Discourses); birthplace Hierapolis in Phrygia; the name epiktetos means “acquired.”
check: Celsus says he spoke “smiling”; the lesson says “quietly” and “calmly.” Confirm.
“A boy from what’s now Turkey grew up enslaved” (Hierapolis; whether he was born a slave is not certain) and “almost two thousand years ago” (c. 50 AD). Confirm.
Paintings show the master holding the ankle before any injury; no break, pain or violence is shown.
